b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.title: Present perfect or past simple?
b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.sub: Two tenses, one question: is the time finished, or connected to now?

b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.h: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Choose between I did and I have done without guessing
Spot the signal words that decide the tense
Avoid the mistake Arabic speakers make with since and for

head: Past simple
Present perfect
rows: Finished time: yesterday, in 2019, last week, two days ago
Unfinished time or no time: today, this year, ever, never, yet, so far
I've lost my keys. (I still can't find them.)
She lived in Paris for five years. (Not now.)
She has lived in Paris for five years. (She still does.)

b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.big: Can you add a finished time, like last year?
b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.p: If yes, use the past simple. If the time is still open, or you don't say when, use the present perfect.

b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.why: ago marks a finished time, so use the past simple.

pairs.note: since needs the present perfect, not the present simple.

b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.why: yet is a present perfect signal word in British English and in exams.

do: Past simple with ago, yesterday, last…, in 2019
Present perfect with ever, never, yet, already, since, for (up to now)
dont: Don't mix have with a finished time
Don't use the present simple with since

points: Finished time → past simple
Connected to now → present perfect
When…? questions ask for a finished time, so use the past simple

b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.title: Everyday phrasal verbs
b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.sub: Twelve verbs you hear every day, and the grammar that holds them together.

b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.p: A verb plus a small word such as up, out, on or off. The meaning often changes completely.

head: Phrasal verb
Meaning
Example
rows: Find out when the train leaves.
I'll pick you up at six.

b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.why: look after = take care of. look for = search.

b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.h: Grammar rule: where does the pronoun go?
b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.big: pick you up ✓   pick up you ✗
b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.p: With pronouns (it, him, you, them), put the pronoun between the verb and the particle. With nouns, both orders work: pick up the kids / pick the kids up.

b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.why: With a pronoun, the particle goes after it: turn it off.

do: Learn each one with an example sentence
give up + -ing: give up smoking
dont: Don't split run out of: run out milk ✗
Don't put a pronoun after the particle

points: The particle changes the meaning
Pronoun in the middle: pick it up
Three-part verbs stay together: run out of

b1-writing-informal-email.title: Writing an informal email
b1-writing-informal-email.sub: Sound warm and natural, not like an office letter.

head: Part
Useful phrases
rows: Thanks for your email. / How are things?
I'm writing to tell you… / Guess what?
Can't wait to hear from you. / Write back soon.

b1-writing-informal-email.q: Which sign-off suits a close friend?
b1-writing-informal-email.why: Yours faithfully is only for formal letters to someone you don't know.

pairs.note: المحترم doesn't translate into English greetings.
Use hope for real wishes. wish is for unreal things.

pairs.bad: I am writing to inform you that…

b1-writing-informal-email.quote:
Hi Sam,
Thanks for your email. It was great to hear about your new job! I'm writing because I've got some news too. I'm coming to London next month for a short course. Are you free on Saturday the 12th? We could have lunch and catch up.
By the way, do you know any cheap places to stay near the centre?
Write back soon.
Love,
Maria

b1-writing-informal-email.q: Which phrase changes the topic informally?
b1-writing-informal-email.why: Furthermore is for essays. By the way is conversational.

do: Give your reason early
Ask a question so your friend replies
dont: Don't use Yours faithfully or I would be grateful if
Don't translate Arabic greetings word for word

points: Greeting → reason → details → closing → sign-off
Contractions make it friendly
Short, warm, clear

b2-conditionals.title: Conditionals: zero to mixed
b2-conditionals.sub: Real or unreal? Present, future or past? Two questions, five patterns.

bullets: Is it about now, the future, or the past?
b2-conditionals.big: The answers choose the tense for you.

head: Type
Form
Example
rows: If you heat ice, it melts.
If it rains, we'll stay home.
If I had time, I'd learn Japanese.
if + past perfect, would have + pp
If I had left earlier, I would have caught the train.
If I had studied medicine, I'd be a doctor now.

b2-conditionals.q: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll cancel the trip.
b2-conditionals.why: Never use will in the if clause, even for the future.

pairs.bad: If I would know, I would tell you.
pairs.good: If I knew, I would tell you.
pairs.note: would belongs in the result clause only.
Use were in exams and formal writing.

b2-conditionals.p: A past condition with a result now:
b2-conditionals.big: If he hadn't missed the flight, he would be here now.
b2-conditionals.note: Look for now or today. They signal a present result.

b2-conditionals.q: If I had saved money, I ___ rich now.
b2-conditionals.why: now = present result, so use would + verb.

head: Normal
Inverted
rows: If I were in your position, …

do: unless = if not: Unless you hurry…
Use were for all persons in unreal conditionals
dont: Don't put will or would after if
Don't say unless you don't (double negative)

points: Real → present / will
Unreal now → past / would
Unreal past → past perfect / would have
Watch for now: it means mixed

b2-collocations-work.title: Collocations for work and study
b2-collocations-work.sub: Why make research sounds wrong, and how to sound fluent instead of translated.

b2-collocations-work.p: Words that naturally go together. Native speakers don't choose them. They hear them thousands of times.
b2-collocations-work.big: meet a deadline · do research · pay attention

head: Collocation
Meaning
rows: accept a duty or the blame

bullets: make = create a result: make a decision, make progress, make a mistake
do = carry out a task: do research, do homework, do a course

b2-collocations-work.why: Research is a task. You do (or carry out) research.

pairs.good: a lot of progress / great progress

b2-collocations-work.why: raise takes an object. rise doesn't.

do: Learn verb + noun as one block
Check whether the noun is uncountable
dont: Don't translate the Arabic verb
Don't say researches, progresses, informations

points: Collocations = sounding fluent
make for results, do for tasks
Uncountable nouns take no a and no -s

b2-opinion-essay.title: Writing an opinion essay
b2-opinion-essay.sub: A clear position, solid reasons, and the linkers examiners look for.

head: Paragraph
Content
rows: Rephrase the question, state your opinion
Topic sentence, explanation, example (plus the opposing view, answered)
Restate your opinion in new words, summarise

b2-opinion-essay.q: Where do you first state your opinion?
b2-opinion-essay.why: The reader needs your position from the start.

head: Job
Linkers
rows: In my view, / I strongly believe that
Furthermore, / In addition, / What is more,
To sum up, / All in all,

pairs.bad: Although it is expensive, but it is useful.
pairs.good: Although it is expensive, it is useful.

pairs.note: according to is for other people's views.

pairs.bad: Cars are useful, however they pollute.
pairs.good: Cars are useful. However, they pollute.

b2-opinion-essay.why: despite + noun / -ing. For a full clause, use although.

do: One clear position from start to finish
A topic sentence at the start of every body paragraph
dont: Don't add new arguments in the conclusion
Don't sit on the fence in an opinion essay

points: Plan before you write: four paragraphs
Use linkers with the right job
Restate, don't repeat, in the conclusion

c1-inversion-for-emphasis.title: Inversion for emphasis
c1-inversion-for-emphasis.sub: Never have I… · Not only did she… · Little did they know…

c1-inversion-for-emphasis.p: After a negative or limiting expression at the start, the word order changes to question order: auxiliary + subject.
c1-inversion-for-emphasis.big: I have never seen → Never have I seen

head: Opening
Example
rows: Rarely have I seen such dedication.
Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.
Hardly had we arrived when it rained.
No sooner had he sat down than the phone rang.
Little did they know what was coming.
Only when I left did I realise.
Under no circumstances should you open it.

c1-inversion-for-emphasis.why: Rarely at the start → auxiliary before subject.

c1-inversion-for-emphasis.h: No auxiliary? Add do / does / did
c1-inversion-for-emphasis.big: She rarely complains → Rarely does she complain.
c1-inversion-for-emphasis.p: After do / does / did, the main verb goes back to its base form: complain, not complains.

c1-inversion-for-emphasis.q: Little ___ that he was being followed.
c1-inversion-for-emphasis.why: After did, use the base form: know.

pairs.bad: Only after the meeting I understood.
pairs.good: Only after the meeting did I understand.

do: Use it in formal writing and speeches for emphasis
No sooner and Hardly go with the past perfect
dont: Don't overuse it. One or two per essay is enough
Don't invert the main verb: Never saw I ✗

points: Negative or limiting opener → question order
Add do/does/did if needed, then the base verb
Only + time phrase: invert the main clause

c1-academic-vocabulary.title: Academic vocabulary for essays
c1-academic-vocabulary.sub: Twelve words that lift your register, and the grammar each one needs.

c1-academic-vocabulary.p: At C1, examiners reward precision. A better word often replaces three weaker ones.

c1-academic-vocabulary.why: mitigate reduces something bad. facilitate makes something easier.

pairs.bad: The app facilitates students to learn.
pairs.note: The object of facilitate is the process.

c1-academic-vocabulary.why: inherent = a permanent part of something.

do: Learn each word with its collocation: substantial evidence
Use them where they are precise, not everywhere
dont: Don't confuse mitigate with militate
Don't stack academic words until the meaning disappears

points: Precision over decoration
Each word has grammar: learn the pattern
Check your nouns: evidence, research and information are uncountable

c1-formal-report.title: Writing a formal report
c1-formal-report.sub: Headings, an impersonal voice, and recommendations someone can act on.

head: Heading
Purpose
rows: Aim of the report and how information was gathered
Specific actions based on the findings

head: Personal
Impersonal
rows: Most people said they liked it.
The majority of respondents expressed satisfaction.
I think we should change the hours.
It is recommended that the opening hours be extended.

c1-formal-report.why: The passive removes the writer and sounds objective.

c1-formal-report.big: It is recommended that new computers be purchased.
c1-formal-report.p: After recommend / suggest / propose that, formal English uses the base form: be, not are or will be.

c1-formal-report.q: It is recommended that the canteen ___ enlarged.

do: Use headings for each section
Support every recommendation with a finding
dont: Don't use contractions or I think
Don't write The aim of this report it is… (double subject)

points: Clear headings, objective tone
Passive and impersonal phrases
Recommendations: specific and justified

c2-cleft-sentences.title: Cleft sentences and fronting
c2-cleft-sentences.sub: Move the spotlight to exactly the part of the sentence that matters.

c2-cleft-sentences.p: It + be + focus + that / who + the rest
c2-cleft-sentences.big: It was Maria who sent the email.
c2-cleft-sentences.note: This suggests someone thought it was another person.

c2-cleft-sentences.q: We met in 2010. → It was in 2010 ___ we met.
c2-cleft-sentences.why: It-clefts use that (or who for people), never what.

c2-cleft-sentences.big: What I need is a long holiday.
bullets: He lied to us. → What he did was lie to us.
Reversed: A long holiday is what I need.

head: Device
Example
rows: All I wanted was a quiet evening.
The reason why it failed is that nobody tested it.
Strange as it may seem, I enjoyed the exam.

c2-cleft-sentences.why: What + subject + did + was + base verb.

pairs.bad: What I need it is rest.
It is the noise what annoys me.
pairs.good: It is the noise that annoys me.

points: It-cleft: contrast or correction
Wh-cleft: build up to the new information
Clefts are never neutral. Use them on purpose.

c2-idioms-and-nuance.title: Idioms and nuance
c2-idioms-and-nuance.sub: At C2, the challenge is choosing the word with exactly the right shade.

head: Idiom
Meaning
rows: enjoy an opportunity, often to criticise

c2-idioms-and-nuance.q: The company says it values diversity but does nothing. It only ___ it.
c2-idioms-and-nuance.why: pay lip service to = support in words only.

pairs.note: Don't translate سلاح ذو حدين word for word.

c2-idioms-and-nuance.q: Everyone knew the budget was the problem, but nobody mentioned ___.
c2-idioms-and-nuance.why: the elephant in the room = an obvious problem that is ignored.

do: Check the register. Many idioms are journalistic.
Keep every word of the idiom exactly
dont: Don't use idioms in formal reports
Don't stack idioms. One well-placed idiom beats five.

points: Idioms are fixed blocks
Nuance = the right word for the reader
Beware sound-alikes: moot / mute, toe / tow

c2-style-and-register.title: Style, register and concision
c2-style-and-register.sub: Every word should earn its place.

head: Wordy
Concise
rows: it is important to note that

c2-style-and-register.q: Concise version of in the event that:

head: Register
Example
rows: The plan fell apart pretty fast.
The initiative proved unsustainable within a short period.

c2-style-and-register.quote: Long sentences build an argument, add the qualifications a careful reader expects, and carry the reader forward. Short ones land it.
c2-style-and-register.p: Alternate them to keep the reader alert.

pairs.bad: The policy… The scheme… This initiative…
pairs.good: The policy… The policy… The policy…
pairs.note: Readers assume a new word means a new thing.

c2-style-and-register.why: go belly up is slang. Neutral uses plain words.

points: Delete what adds nothing
Match the register to the reader
Keep key terms consistent
